text: Meet the ESP32. A tiny computer you program. Its first job: blink a blue light.
Build a traffic light. Three LEDs, three resistors and a few wires. Your code runs red, green and yellow, and the cars obey.
Make your own patterns. Change the code, change the lights.
Teach it to listen. Add a button. Press it and the cars get red, so the walker can cross.
A fair crossing. A tap is remembered: WAIT lights up, the green finishes, then people cross safely.
Build it yourself. Every wire, hole and line of code comes with a “why”.

Meet your ESP32. This little board will be the brain of every project in this course: a traffic light, a buzzer, even something you control from a phone. Today you’re a pin detective. You’ll explore the board, find its secrets, and learn the real words engineers use. Each mission unlocks a maker word.
Find the brain. Every computer has a brain that runs the program. On this board the brain hides under a shiny metal lid.

where: 00-meet-esp32 · How does it reach the internet?
text: How does it reach the internet? Your ESP32 can join Wi-Fi without any wires. To do that, it needs something that sends and catches invisible radio waves.
Wake it up. Right now the board is asleep: it has no power. Where would you plug in a cable to give it power and send it your code?
Count the legs. See the two rows of metal legs? They are called pins, and they connect the board to wires, lights and sensors. Each one has a name printed next to it.

Find the road home. Electricity is like a runner on a loop: it leaves the board, does its job (like lighting an LED), and must come back home. No way home, no light! The way home is called ground, and the board prints it as GND.

Find the power pins. Two pins give electricity to other parts. One gives a gentle 3.3 volts, printed 3V3. One brings in about 5 volts from the USB cable, printed VIN. A volt measures how hard electricity pushes, like water pressure in a pipe.
Wake up the blue LED. There’s a tiny blue light on the board, and it’s wired to pin D2. Your program can switch that pin on and off. That’s what most pins are for!
The name trick. Here’s a secret that confuses lots of grown-ups. In code we write a GPIO number, like Pin(25). Where is pin 25? Count along the board… or is there a better way?

Pins with a special job. A few pins already have a job, like talking to your computer, restarting the board, or only listening. They’re now orange. Good engineers check a pin’s job before they use it.
Pin hunt! Time to prove your detective skills. Officer Ohm calls out a pin and you find it, fast!
Detective quiz. Three quick questions and the Pin Detective badge is yours.

Your first circuit. Today you’ll build a real light with your own hands. No code at all! Everything you need is on the table: a breadboard, a red LED, a resistor and some jumper wires. Your ESP32 will give the power.
Secret tunnels. The breadboard hides metal strips under its holes. Holes on the same strip are joined, so electricity can travel between them. Tap some holes to find the hidden strips!
Meet the LED. An LED is a tiny light. Look closely: one leg is long and one is short. That matters! Electricity can only go through an LED one way: in through the long leg, out through the short leg.

Meet the resistor. A resistor slows electricity down, like a narrow part of a water pipe. Without one, too much electricity rushes through the LED and can break it. The colour bands tell you how strong it is.

Safety first: unplug. Engineers have a golden rule: never change wires while the board has power. One wrong hole could make a short circuit. Your ESP32 is still plugged in from Pin Detective. See its red power light?

Place the resistor. Put the resistor across the middle gap, in column 7: one leg above the gap and one leg below. Why across the gap? Then electricity arriving at the top strip can only reach the bottom strip by going through the resistor.
Place the LED. Now the LED. Its long leg goes in the same strip as the resistor’s bottom leg: column 7, below the gap. The short leg goes next door, in column 8.
The road home, part 1. Electricity that leaves the LED’s short leg needs a road home to GND. First, a short black wire from the short leg’s strip to the blue − rail.
The road home, part 2. The − rail isn’t joined to the ESP32 yet. A long black wire joins the rail to a GND pin, and the road home is complete.

Power goes in last. Last wire: the red one brings the power. It goes from 3V3 (3.3 volts, always on) to column 7 above the gap, the resistor’s top strip. We connect power last, so nothing can get power until the whole circuit is ready.

Check, then plug in. Before power, engineers check every connection. Follow the path with your finger: 3V3, red wire, resistor, LED, black wire, − rail, black wire, GND. All good? Then it’s time to plug in!
The fix-it shop. Officer Ohm’s friends built the same circuit three times, but each light stays dark. Can you find each problem? Tap the part that’s wrong.
Build it for real. Time to build it on your real breadboard, exactly like on the screen. Use the same holes, and ask an adult to check before you plug in.
Lab quiz. Three quick questions and the Circuit Lab 1 badge is yours.
